\(\LaTeX\)
Accessible PDFs require tagging. For LaTeX, this means adding \DocumentMetadata{tagging=on} before \documentclass and requires installing some packages.1

Normally, when rendering qmd to PDF via LaTeX, we can add lines to the LaTeX preamble with include-in-header: in the YAML header. But adding lines before \documentclass causes an error:
 pdf: 
   include-in-header: 
     - text: |
        \DocumentMetadata{tagging=on} # DOES NOT WORK!  
        \documentclass{article}
Thus, I believe a LaTeX template is required to allow tagging when rendering qmd documents as PDFs via LaTeX.

text:
Website navigation buttons
Issue:

Critical: Ensure an element’s role supports its ARIA attributes


.navbar

This seems to be related to how the navigation bar is constructed (by Quarto defaults, I did not modify this):
The HTML originally included:
aria-controls="navbarCollapse" role="menu" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle navigation"
GPT’s response:

The role=“menu” is usually reserved for a list of menu items (think dropdown menus for accessibility, not a toggle button). You’re probably applying role=“menu” to the navbar toggle button, which is incorrect per ARIA standards. ARIA attribute permissions:


aria-expanded makes sense for interactive elements like a button, a link, or something toggling visibility. aria-label=“Toggle navigation” is fine for such a toggle. role=“menu” is not appropriate for a toggle button—it is used for containers of menu items, not the toggle itself. Common toggle buttons should have role=“button”, not role=“menu”.


Accessibility checkers will flag this combo because: aria-expanded, aria-label, and aria-controls are meant for elements like buttons. role=“menu” does not support these attributes (see W3C ARIA roles reference).

This issue seems to have been fixed by the same fix as the next.

text:
“div” vs. “main”
Issue:

Moderate: Ensure all page content is contained by landmarks

From GPT:

Quarto’s default template uses <div id="quarto-content"> instead of <main id="quarto-content">. Your accessibility checker wants your main content inside a <main> — the most robust, semantically correct landmark.


How to Fix It: Override the HTML Template by creating a custom HTML template for your Quarto site. You can replace the <div> with <main>.

Fix:
This issue seems to have been fixed by adding <script> to assets/accessibility-fixes.js.

Ford School Inclusivity Statement: Members of the Ford School community represent a rich variety of backgrounds and perspectives. We are committed to providing an atmosphere for learning that respects these differences. While working together to build this community we ask all members to:

share their unique experiences, values and beliefs

be open to the views of others

honor the uniqueness of their colleagues

appreciate the opportunity that we have to learn from each other in this community

value one another’s opinions and communicate in a respectful manner

keep confidential discussions that the community has of a personal (or professional) nature

use this opportunity together to discuss ways in which we can create an inclusive environment in Ford classes and across the UM community

Student Mental Health and Wellbeing: The University of Michigan is committed to advancing the mental health and wellbeing of its students. We acknowledge that a variety of issues can directly impact students’ academic performance and overall wellbeing. If you or someone you know is feeling overwhelmed, depressed, and/or in need of support, services are available.
You may access the Ford School’s embedded counselor Paige Ziegler (pziegler@umich.edu) and/or counselors and urgent services at Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) and/or University Health Service (UHS). Students may also use the Crisis Text Line (text ‘4UMICH’ to 741741) to be connected to a trained crisis volunteer.
Accommodations for Students with Disabilities: The University of Michigan is committed to creating as accessible educational environment for students with disabilities as possible.
If you anticipate or are experiencing barriers based on disability or temporary injuries, Services for Students with Disabilities (SSD) (ssd.umich.edu) is the office that students work with to explore reasonable accommodations, tools, and resources.

If you are already connected with SSD and have approved accommodations, please share your letter through Accommodate as soon as possible so that we can discuss how your accommodations will be implemented in this course. The sooner I know about your disability access-needs, the more equipped I can be to facilitate accommodations. You should reach out to me and/or your Disability Access Coordinator if you have any questions or concerns about your accommodations.

If you have not connected with SSD and anticipate or are experiencing a disability-related barrier, and would like to discuss accommodations and/or resources, please contact SSD by completing their initial information form (https://ssd.umich.edu/)

If you have a temporary medical injury/condition, such as a broken arm, I may be able to assist in minimizing classroom barriers. In situations where additional assistance is needed, you should contact the SSD as noted above.

Academic Integrity: The Ford School academic community, like all communities, functions best when its members treat one another with honesty, fairness, respect, and trust. We hold all members of our community to high standards of scholarship and integrity. To accomplish its mission of providing an optimal educational environment and developing leaders of society, the Ford School promotes the assumption of personal responsibility and integrity and prohibits all forms of academic dishonesty, plagiarism and misconduct. Academic dishonesty may be understood as any action or attempted action that may result in creating an unfair academic advantage for oneself or an unfair academic advantage or disadvantage for any other member or members of the academic community. Plagiarism involves representing the words, ideas, or work of others as one’s own in writing or presentations, and failing to give full and proper credit to the original source. Conduct, without regard to motive, that violates the academic integrity and ethical standards will result in serious consequences and disciplinary action. The Ford School’s policy of academic integrity can be found in the BA, MPP, and PhD Program handbooks. Additional information regarding academic dishonesty, plagiarism and misconduct and their consequences is available on the Rackham website.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
When \(y\) Has Limited Values

We often have cases where \(y\) is dichotomous or comes in nominal/ordinal categories.
In these cases, OLS can be problematic:


OLS gives continuous predicted values that may be hard to interpret.
OLS can give predicted values that lie outside the range of the dependent variable.
The effect of any \(x_i\) on the outcome may not be linear across its range.
Heterodskedasticity is pretty much automatic.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Maximum Likelihood Approaches

For dichotomous data, we have probit/logit which use different probability distributions but produce similar results
For nominal data (i.e. unordered categories), we can use multinomial logit or probit.
For ordinal data, we can use ordered logit or probit.
In general: interpretation is the key. It is much trickier than OLS; the coefficients do not directly tell us the magnitude of change.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Example: Bias in Policy Professionals

Banuri et al. (2018) study whether policy professionals are subject to cognitive biases.
e.g. confirmation bias, when people remember or prefer information that conforms to prior views.
The survey sample consists of employees in the World Bank and DFID selected randomly and recruited via email.
The survey contained an experiment that randomized participants into one of two scenarios.
The outcome variable, measured in each scenario, is dichotomous.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
The Two Scenarios
Participants see the same data but the scenario differs:

Control group: a non-ideological scenario involving a study about the effectiveness of a skin cream.
Treatment group: study about the effects for the bottom 40% of the income distribution when localities raise the minimum wage.
Are people in the treatment group more likely to interpret the data incorrectly?
Due to ideological predisposition, people in the treatment group might be more inclined to see what they want in the results.

Above, the correct answer is that action Y is better, but this differs depending on the randomization.
The dependent variable is 1 if the person interprets the results correctly, and 0 otherwise.

text:
Dichotomous Data: Linear Probability Model
Actually, we could just use OLS despite a dichotomous \(y\).
\[\begin{align*}
\mathop{\mathrm{E}}[y_i|\mathbf{x_i}] & = [1 \times \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1|\mathbf{x_i})] + [0 \times \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 0)|\mathbf{x_i}]\\
&  = \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1|\mathbf{x_i})
\end{align*}\]
We can rewrite the expected value of \(y_i\) given \(\mathbf{x_i}\) as:
\[\begin{equation*}
\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1|\mathbf{x_i}) = \mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}
\end{equation*}\]
Where \(\mathbf{x_i}\) is a \(1 \times k\) row vector from the matrix \(\mathbf X\), and \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is a \(k \times 1\) column vector.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Interpretation

The interpretation is similar to OLS. Each one-unit increase in \(x\) leads to a \(\beta\)-sized change in the probability that \(y\) equals 1.
Problem: it’s unrealistic that \(x\) has the same, linear effect on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1)\) regardless of its starting level.

the estimated effect of \(x\) is biased for some values of \(x\).

Problem: predictions outside the boundaries of 0 and 1 are possible.
Problem: heteroskedasticity in the prediction errors. The errors are not normal, either.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Generalization to Multiple Independent Variables
\[\begin{align*}
\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1|\mathbf{x_i}) & = \mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}\\
& = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1}  + \ldots + \beta_{k-1}x_{k-1} %+ \epsilon_i
\end{align*}\]

Everything is the same. The inner product \(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is a scalar.
We can interpret each \(\beta_{k}\) as the predicted change in the probability that \(y_{i} = 1\) associated with a one-unit change in \(x_{k}\).
All the same problems are still present.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
In Defense of the LPM

The coefficients are easy to interpret and explain.
There are scenarios where a probit/logit cannot be estimated but an LPM can:

e.g. when an independent dummy variable is perfectly correlated with the outcome.

Standard errors in a logistic model can be too small.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
section: The LPM Works Well in RCT Setup
text:
The LPM Works Well in RCT Setup

In an RCT with a dichotomous outcome, the LPM provides a consistent estimator of the average treatment effect. \[\begin{equation*}
y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}T + \beta_{2}x
\end{equation*}\]
In the above, both \(y\) and \(T\) are dichotomous, and \(\beta_{1}\) is the estimated treatment effect.
Linearity doesn’t matter, since \(T\) has only two values. Also, \(x\) is uncorrelated with \(T\) due to random assignment.
In this setup, the marginal effect of \(T\) on average across the range of \(x\) is the same as in a probit/logit model.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
section: Binary Response Models: Probit and Logit
text:
Binary Response Models: Probit and Logit

These techniques use an S-shaped curve that is bounded between 0 and 1 to fit the data.

Probit: based on the cumulative normal distribution.
Logit: based on the cumulative logistic distribution.

In both, we think of the observed, dichotomous \(y\) as being generated by a latent, continuous variable \(y^{*}\).
\[\begin{equation*}
  y_{i}=\begin{cases}
    1 & \text{if } y^{*}_{i} > \tau \\
    0 & \text{if } y^{*}_{i} \leq \tau
  \end{cases}
\end{equation*}\]
These are called link functions because they link \(y^{*}\) to \(y\).

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Choosing the Distribution Function
\[\begin{equation*}
y_{i}^{*} = \mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}+ \epsilon_{i}
\end{equation*}\]

There aren’t strong reasons to choose probit over logit or vice-versa. They yield equivalent results.
In both, we model \(y_{i}^{*}\) as a linear function of the \(x_i\)’s.
With probit, we assume standard normal errors: \(\epsilon_{i} \sim N(0,1)\)
With logit, we assume logistic errors: \(\epsilon_{i} \sim \lambda(0,\frac{\pi^2}{3})\)

Logit has slightly fatter tails due to the greater variance.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Probit: Cumulative Normal Density Function
\[\begin{equation*}
\Phi(\epsilon) = \int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon} \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{(t - \mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} \right) dt
\end{equation*}\]
which, since we assume \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma =1\), simplifies to:
\[\begin{equation*}
\Phi(\epsilon) = \int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2} \right) dt
\end{equation*}\]
Here we use the cumulative normal density to get the area under the normal distribution up to \(\epsilon\).

Since \(y_{i}^{*} = \mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}+ \epsilon_{i}\), there is some probability that \(y_i^* < \tau\) once \(\epsilon_i\) is added on.
We can use the fact that \(\epsilon\) is assumed to have a standard normal distribution to find the area above/below the threshold.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Probit Analysis
We use the latent variable \(y^{*}\) and the cumulative normal density to calculate \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_{i} = 1 | \mathbf{x_{i}})\), setting \(\tau = 0\). \[\begin{align*}
\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y = 1 | \mathbf x_{i}) & =  \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y^{*} > 0 | \mathbf x_{i})\\[.2em]
    & = \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}+ \epsilon > 0 | \mathbf x_{i})\\[.2em]
    & = \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(\epsilon > -\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mathbf x_{i})\\[.2em]
    & = \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(\epsilon \leq \mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mathbf x_{i})\\[.2em]
    & = \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})
\end{align*}\] The probability that \(y_{i}=1\) is given by the cumulative normal distribution evaluated at the value \(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}\).

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Log Likelihood Function
\[\begin{align*}
L(\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{X}) & = \prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\\
& = \prod_{y=1}\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_{i} =1|\mathbf{x_{i}}) \prod_{y=0}[1 - \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_{i} =1|\mathbf{x_{i}})]\\
& = \prod_{y=1} \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}) \prod_{y=0}[1 - \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})]\\
\end{align*}\]
Which makes the log likelihood function: \[\begin{equation*}
\ln L(\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{X}) = \sum_{y=1} \ln \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}) + \sum_{y=0}\ln[1 - \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})]
\end{equation*}\]

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Estimation of a Probit

The MLE finds the values of the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) that maximize the given log likelihood.
We get a set of coefficients just like usual. The interpretation is different, however.
Stata: probit y x1 x2 x3
R: model <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, family = binomial(link = "probit"), data = mydata)

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Interpretation of Coefficients

The sign of the coefficient indicates the direction of the relationship between the \(x\)’s and \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\).
To understand the magnitude of the effect, we must determine by how much \(\Phi(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta})\) changes in response to a particular \(x_i\).
This effect depends upon the values of all the variables in the analysis, since the starting point on the S-shaped curve matters.
There is no direct way to interpret the magnitude of the change in probability due to change in a single \(x_i\) without considering the values of the other \(x_i\)’s.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
section: Different Ways to Interpret Probit Results
text:
Different Ways to Interpret Probit Results

Predicted Probability. Calculate \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\) given the values of the \(x\)’s for a particular case of interest.
Change in Predicted Probability. Calculate the change in \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\) when \(x\)’s change from one set of values to another.
Marginal Effect. The predicted effect on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\) from changing one \(x_{i}\), starting at specified values for the \(x\)’s.
Average Marginal Effect. The average effect on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\) from changing one \(x_{i}\), calculated across all the cases in the sample.

Each case is evaluated at its own values for the \(x\)’s.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Calculating a Predicted Probability
The probability of a vote for Biden is \(\Phi(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta})\). If PoliticalNews=2, Ideology=3, FauciTherm=65, BLMtherm=60, and BAplus=1 then:
\[\begin{align*}
\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}& = -1.472 + .150(\text{PoliticalNews}) - .472(\text{Ideology})\\
&  + .022(\text{FauciTherm}) + .023(\text{BLMtherm}) + .155(\text{BAplus})\\[.4em]
& = -1.47 + .15(2) - .472(3) + .022(65) + .023(60) + .155(1)\\[.4em]
  & = .377
\end{align*}\]
To find the probability that a person with the above characteristics voted for Biden, evaluate using the cumulative normal distribution: \(\Phi(.377) = .65\).

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Evaluating Cumulative Normal with Software
\(\Phi(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta})\) is the area under the normal density up to the point \(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}\). We can find it in these ways:

Stata: display normal(xB)
R: pnorm(xB)
Excel: =NORM.DIST(xB, 0, 1, TRUE)

Where xB is the value of the point we want to evaluate: \(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}\)

Commands for Predicted Values

The margins command in Stata can calculate predicted probabilities or the value of \(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}\).
The default option for predict is the predicted probability. Add xb in the parentheses to get \(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) instead.

margins, predict() at(var1=3 var2=10 var3=25)
margins, predict(xb) at(var1=3 var2=10 var3=25)

The value of each independent variable must be specified. For each var, you must use the name of a variable in the model.
For R, the marginaleffects library provides the predictions function.

In Stata, one can also obtain the predicted probabilities for each case in the sample with the predict command.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Finding the Effect of \(\Delta x_k\)

Let the initial predicted value be \(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}\).
Then, by changing \(x_k\) to some new value, we can calculate \(\mathbf{\tilde{x}_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}\).
The predicted effect of the change in \(x_k\) on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1)\) is given by: \[\begin{equation*}
\Phi(\mathbf{\tilde{x}_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}) - \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})
\end{equation*}\]
The values of all the variables in the analysis are relevant.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Example
Previously we found that the probability of a Biden vote is .65. What if we change Ideology from 3 to 5?
\[\begin{align*}
\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}& = -1.472 + .150(\text{PoliticalNews}) - .472(\text{Ideology})\\
&  + .022(\text{FauciTherm}) + .023(\text{BLMtherm}) + .155(\text{BAplus})\\[.1em]
& = -1.47 + .15(2) - .472(5) + .022(65) + .023(60) + .155(1)\\[.1em]
  & = -.567
\end{align*}\]
Since \(\Phi(-.567) = .29\), we can calculate the effect of the change in Ideology like this: \[\begin{equation*}
\Phi(-.567) - \Phi(.377)= .29 - .65 \ = \ -.36
\end{equation*}\] The probability of a Biden vote falls by .36 to .29.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Marginal Effect of \(x_k\)
As with OLS, we can find the marginal effect of \(x_k\) by taking the derivative with respect to \(x_k\). \[\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y=1|\mathbf{x})}{\partial x_k} = \frac{\partial \Phi(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial x_k} = \phi(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta})\beta_k
\end{equation*}\] where \(\phi(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta})\) is the normal probability density function (note: this is not the cumulative density function!).

For the example case when Ideology=3, \(\phi(.377)=.372\).
Recall that the coefficient on Ideology is -.472.
Since \((.372)(-.472)  = -.176\), the marginal effect of a one-unit change in Ideology is about -.18 for \(x\)’s set at these values.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Measures of Fit

In OLS, typical measures of the model’s fit include the \(F\)-statistic and the \(R^2\) statistic.
For probit analysis, the correlate to the \(F\)-test is a likelihood ratio (LR) test. The idea is the same: the null hypothesis is that all coefficients are zero.
The “pseudo-\(R^2\)” measure should be treated with caution. It’s not that useful a statistic.
What would be better? The percentage of cases predicted correctly. Use the estat command.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
The Likelihood Ratio (LR) Test

The test involves a comparison of the likelihood of the estimated model to the likelihood of a restricted model.
In the restricted model, the coefficients on the \(x_i\)’s are restricted to 0. This is an intercept-only model (Iteration 0 in the MLE).
A statistically significant increase in the likelihood in the unrestricted model means that the \(x_i\)’s have explanatory power. \[\begin{equation*}
LR = -2 \ln\left(\frac{L_r}{L_{ur}}\right) = -2(\ln L_r - \ln L_{ur})
\end{equation*}\]
The LR statistic has a \(\chi^2\) distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restricted coefficients.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
LR Test for Joint Significance

We can also use an LR test to determine whether two or more coefficients are jointly significant.
For the restricted model, obtain the final log likelihood of the model estimated without including these \(x_i\)’s.
For the unrestricted model, use the final log likelihood of the full model. \[\begin{equation*}
LR = -2(\ln L_r - \ln L_{ur})
\end{equation*}\]
The LR statistic has a \(\chi^2\) distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restricted coefficients.

Basics of Logit

An odds ratio is the probability of an outcome divided by its complement (i.e. the probability that it will not happen).
Logit uses the log of odds ratio for modeling \(y^*\) \[\begin{equation*}
\ln \left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right) = \mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}+ \epsilon_{i}
\end{equation*}\]
The odds ratio is: \(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\). Taking the natural log makes it linear.
The coefficients thus give us changes in the log odds ratio. We can convert this into changes into predicted probabilities.

Finding the Effect of \(\Delta x_k\)

Quite similar to probit, the predicted effect of the change in \(x_k\) on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1)\) is given by: \[\begin{equation*}
\Lambda(\mathbf{\tilde{x}_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}) - \Lambda(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})
\end{equation*}\]
The values of all the variables in the analysis are relevant.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Example
Previously we found that the probability of a Biden vote is .68. What if we change Ideology from 3 to 5? \[\begin{align*}
\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}& = -2.691 + .295(\text{PoliticalNews}) - .898(\text{Ideology})\\
&  + .041(\text{FauciTherm}) + .043(\text{BLMtherm}) + .282(\text{BAplus})\\[.4em]
& = -2.269 + .295(2) - .898(5) + .041(65) + .043(60) + .281(1)\\[.4em]
  & = -1.063
\end{align*}\] Since \(\Lambda(-1.063)\)= .26, we can calculate the effect of the specified change in Ideology: \[\begin{equation*}
\Lambda(-1.063) - \Lambda(.733)= .26 - .68 \ = \ -.42
\end{equation*}\]
The probability of a Biden vote falls by .42 to .26.

Interpretation with Odds Ratios
Since the model in linear in \(\beta_{k}\): \[\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial \ln \Omega(x)}{\partial x_{k}} = \beta_{k}
\end{equation*}\]

A one-unit change in \(x_{k}\) is associated with a \(\beta_{k}\) change in the log odds ratio.
Thus, a one-unit change in \(x_{k}\) is associated with an \(\exp(\beta_{k})\) change in the odds ratio.
If \(\exp(\beta_{k}) >1\), the odds are \(\exp(\beta_{k})\) times larger. If \(\exp(\beta_{k}) <1\), the odds are \(\exp(\beta_{k})\) times smaller.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Logistic Regression

We can get the coefficients reported as the changes in the odds ratios using the logistic command, rather than logit.
In other words, where logit gives us \(\beta_{k}\), logistic will give us a coefficient that equals \(\exp(\beta_{k})\).
If we use the logistic command but add the option coef, we get the same coefficients as the logit command.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Logistic Regression with Odds Ratios





A one-unit increase in Ideology is associated with decreasing the odds of voting for Biden by a factor of .4073.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Key for Interpretation

Odds ratios can never be negative. Rather than be centered around 0, they are centered around 1.
Why? Because if a ratio is multiplied by 1, it does not change.
Thus, a variable has a negative effect on the odds of the outcome if the change in the ratio is less than 1.
A variable has a positive effect if the odds ratio changes by a factor greater than 1.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Example

Suppose the initial odds of a person voting for Biden are 7 to 3. That is an odds ratio of 2.333 and a probability of \(\frac{7}{7 + 3}\) or .70.
If Ideology increases by 1, the odds ratio would change by a factor of .4073, making it \((2.333)(.4073) = .9052\).
That’s odds of .9052 to 1, which is about .48 in probability terms: \[\begin{equation*}
\frac{.9052}{.9052 + 1} \approx .48
\end{equation*}\]
Predicted probabilities are probably easier to interpret, but some disciplines (e.g. public health) tend to use odds ratios.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Advice

Within the same model, odds ratios do have some value in communicating relative risk for different groups.
Even in fields like health research, however, the use of odds ratios is under question (e.g. article by Norton et al.).
Odds ratios are not comparable across different models or studies.
Predicted probabilities and marginal effects are much more understandable to most audiences.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Concluding Points

With dichotomous dependent variables, both the LPM and probit/logit models have virtues.
Probit/logit models are better for unbiased predictions of marginal effects for specific hypothetical cases.
The LPM offers easier interpretation of coefficients.
When RCTs have a dichotomous DV, the LPM is just fine.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
When \(y\) Has Limited Values

We often have cases where \(y\) is dichotomous or comes in nominal/ordinal categories.
In these cases, OLS can be problematic:


OLS gives continuous predicted values that may be hard to interpret.
OLS can give predicted values that lie outside the range of the dependent variable.
The effect of any \(x_i\) on the outcome may not be linear across its range.
Heterodskedasticity is pretty much automatic.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Maximum Likelihood Approaches

For dichotomous data, we have probit/logit which use different probability distributions but produce similar results
For nominal data (i.e. unordered categories), we can use multinomial logit or probit.
For ordinal data, we can use ordered logit or probit.
In general: interpretation is the key. It is much trickier than OLS; the coefficients do not directly tell us the magnitude of change.

text:

Banuri et al. (2018) study whether policy professionals are subject to cognitive biases.
e.g. confirmation bias, when people remember or prefer information that conforms to prior views.
The survey sample consists of employees in the World Bank and DFID selected randomly and recruited via email.
The survey contained an experiment that randomized participants into one of two scenarios.
The outcome variable, measured in each scenario, is dichotomous.

Participants see the same data but the scenario differs:

Control group: a non-ideological scenario involving a study about the effectiveness of a skin cream.

Are people in the treatment group more likely to interpret the data incorrectly?
Due to ideological predisposition, people in the treatment group might be more inclined to see what they want in the results.

Dichotomous Data: Linear Probability Model
Actually, we could just use OLS despite a dichotomous \(y\).
\[\begin{align*}
\mathop{\mathrm{E}}[y_i|\mathbf{x_i}] & = [1 \times \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1|\mathbf{x_i})] + [0 \times \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 0)|\mathbf{x_i}]\\
&  = \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1|\mathbf{x_i})
\end{align*}\]
We can rewrite the expected value of \(y_i\) given \(\mathbf{x_i}\) as:
\[\begin{equation*}
\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1|\mathbf{x_i}) = \mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}
\end{equation*}\]
Where \(\mathbf{x_i}\) is a \(1 \times k\) row vector from the matrix \(\mathbf X\), and \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is a \(k \times 1\) column vector.

Interpretation

The interpretation is similar to OLS. Each one-unit increase in \(x\) leads to a \(\beta\)-sized change in the probability that \(y\) equals 1.
Problem: it’s unrealistic that \(x\) has the same, linear effect on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1)\) regardless of its starting level.

the estimated effect of \(x\) is biased for some values of \(x\).

Problem: predictions outside the boundaries of 0 and 1 are possible.
Problem: heteroskedasticity in the prediction errors. The errors are not normal, either.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Generalization to Multiple Independent Variables
\[\begin{align*}
\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1|\mathbf{x_i}) & = \mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}\\
& = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{1}  + \ldots + \beta_{k-1}x_{k-1} %+ \epsilon_i
\end{align*}\]

Everything is the same. The inner product \(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is a scalar.
We can interpret each \(\beta_{k}\) as the predicted change in the probability that \(y_{i} = 1\) associated with a one-unit change in \(x_{k}\).
All the same problems are still present.

In Defense of the LPM

The coefficients are easy to interpret and explain.
There are scenarios where a probit/logit cannot be estimated but an LPM can:

e.g. when an independent dummy variable is perfectly correlated with the outcome.

Standard errors in a logistic model can be too small.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
section: The LPM Works Well in RCT Setup
text:
The LPM Works Well in RCT Setup

In an RCT with a dichotomous outcome, the LPM provides a consistent estimator of the average treatment effect. \[\begin{equation*}
y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}T + \beta_{2}x
\end{equation*}\]
In the above, both \(y\) and \(T\) are dichotomous, and \(\beta_{1}\) is the estimated treatment effect.
Linearity doesn’t matter, since \(T\) has only two values. Also, \(x\) is uncorrelated with \(T\) due to random assignment.
In this setup, the marginal effect of \(T\) on average across the range of \(x\) is the same as in a probit/logit model.

section: Binary Response Models: Probit and Logit
text:
Binary Response Models: Probit and Logit

These techniques use an S-shaped curve that is bounded between 0 and 1 to fit the data.

Probit: based on the cumulative normal distribution.
Logit: based on the cumulative logistic distribution.

In both, we think of the observed, dichotomous \(y\) as being generated by a latent, continuous variable \(y^{*}\).
\[\begin{equation*}
  y_{i}=\begin{cases}
    1 & \text{if } y^{*}_{i} > \tau \\
    0 & \text{if } y^{*}_{i} \leq \tau
  \end{cases}
\end{equation*}\]
These are called link functions because they link \(y^{*}\) to \(y\).

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Choosing the Distribution Function
\[\begin{equation*}
y_{i}^{*} = \mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}+ \epsilon_{i}
\end{equation*}\]

There aren’t strong reasons to choose probit over logit or vice-versa. They yield equivalent results.
In both, we model \(y_{i}^{*}\) as a linear function of the \(x_i\)’s.
With probit, we assume standard normal errors: \(\epsilon_{i} \sim N(0,1)\)
With logit, we assume logistic errors: \(\epsilon_{i} \sim \lambda(0,\frac{\pi^2}{3})\)

Logit has slightly fatter tails due to the greater variance.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Probit: Cumulative Normal Density Function
\[\begin{equation*}
\Phi(\epsilon) = \int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon} \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{(t - \mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}} \right) dt
\end{equation*}\]
which, since we assume \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma =1\), simplifies to:
\[\begin{equation*}
\Phi(\epsilon) = \int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2} \right) dt
\end{equation*}\]
Here we use the cumulative normal density to get the area under the normal distribution up to \(\epsilon\).

We can use the fact that \(\epsilon\) is assumed to have a standard normal distribution to find the area above/below the threshold.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Probit Analysis
We use the latent variable \(y^{*}\) and the cumulative normal density to calculate \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_{i} = 1 | \mathbf{x_{i}})\), setting \(\tau = 0\). \[\begin{align*}
\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y = 1 | \mathbf x_{i}) & =  \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y^{*} > 0 | \mathbf x_{i})\\[.2em]
    & = \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}+ \epsilon > 0 | \mathbf x_{i})\\[.2em]
    & = \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(\epsilon > -\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mathbf x_{i})\\[.2em]
    & = \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(\epsilon \leq \mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mathbf x_{i})\\[.2em]
    & = \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})
\end{align*}\] The probability that \(y_{i}=1\) is given by the cumulative normal distribution evaluated at the value \(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}\).

Log Likelihood Function
\[\begin{align*}
L(\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{X}) & = \prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\\
& = \prod_{y=1}\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_{i} =1|\mathbf{x_{i}}) \prod_{y=0}[1 - \mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_{i} =1|\mathbf{x_{i}})]\\
& = \prod_{y=1} \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}) \prod_{y=0}[1 - \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})]\\
\end{align*}\]
Which makes the log likelihood function: \[\begin{equation*}
\ln L(\boldsymbol{\beta}| \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{X}) = \sum_{y=1} \ln \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}) + \sum_{y=0}\ln[1 - \Phi(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})]
\end{equation*}\]

The MLE finds the values of the parameters \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) that maximize the given log likelihood.
We get a set of coefficients just like usual. The interpretation is different, however.

Interpretation of Coefficients

The sign of the coefficient indicates the direction of the relationship between the \(x\)’s and \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\).
To understand the magnitude of the effect, we must determine by how much \(\Phi(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta})\) changes in response to a particular \(x_i\).
This effect depends upon the values of all the variables in the analysis, since the starting point on the S-shaped curve matters.
There is no direct way to interpret the magnitude of the change in probability due to change in a single \(x_i\) without considering the values of the other \(x_i\)’s.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
section: Different Ways to Interpret Probit Results
text:
Different Ways to Interpret Probit Results

Predicted Probability. Calculate \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\) given the values of the \(x\)’s for a particular case of interest.
Change in Predicted Probability. Calculate the change in \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\) when \(x\)’s change from one set of values to another.
Marginal Effect. The predicted effect on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\) from changing one \(x_{i}\), starting at specified values for the \(x\)’s.
Average Marginal Effect. The average effect on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i=1)\) from changing one \(x_{i}\), calculated across all the cases in the sample.

Each case is evaluated at its own values for the \(x\)’s.

& = -1.47 + .15(2) - .472(3) + .022(65) + .023(60) + .155(1)\\[.4em]

\end{align*}\]

\Phi(-.567) - \Phi(.377)= .29 - .65 \ = \ -.36

text:
Measures of Fit

In OLS, typical measures of the model’s fit include the \(F\)-statistic and the \(R^2\) statistic.
For probit analysis, the correlate to the \(F\)-test is a likelihood ratio (LR) test. The idea is the same: the null hypothesis is that all coefficients are zero.
The “pseudo-\(R^2\)” measure should be treated with caution. It’s not that useful a statistic.
What would be better? The percentage of cases predicted correctly. Use the estat command.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
The Likelihood Ratio (LR) Test

The test involves a comparison of the likelihood of the estimated model to the likelihood of a restricted model.
In the restricted model, the coefficients on the \(x_i\)’s are restricted to 0. This is an intercept-only model (Iteration 0 in the MLE).
A statistically significant increase in the likelihood in the unrestricted model means that the \(x_i\)’s have explanatory power. \[\begin{equation*}
LR = -2 \ln\left(\frac{L_r}{L_{ur}}\right) = -2(\ln L_r - \ln L_{ur})
\end{equation*}\]
The LR statistic has a \(\chi^2\) distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restricted coefficients.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
LR Test for Joint Significance

We can also use an LR test to determine whether two or more coefficients are jointly significant.
For the restricted model, obtain the final log likelihood of the model estimated without including these \(x_i\)’s.
For the unrestricted model, use the final log likelihood of the full model. \[\begin{equation*}
LR = -2(\ln L_r - \ln L_{ur})
\end{equation*}\]
The LR statistic has a \(\chi^2\) distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restricted coefficients.

Basics of Logit

An odds ratio is the probability of an outcome divided by its complement (i.e. the probability that it will not happen).
Logit uses the log of odds ratio for modeling \(y^*\) \[\begin{equation*}
\ln \left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right) = \mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}+ \epsilon_{i}
\end{equation*}\]
The odds ratio is: \(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\). Taking the natural log makes it linear.
The coefficients thus give us changes in the log odds ratio. We can convert this into changes into predicted probabilities.

text: Logit Results from Same Example

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Example Interpretation (Logit)
The probability of a vote for Biden is \(\Lambda(\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta})\). If PoliticalNews=2, Ideology=3, FauciTherm=65, BLMtherm=60, and BAplus=1: \[\begin{align*}
\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}& = -2.691 + .295(\text{PoliticalNews}) - .898(\text{Ideology})\\
&  + .041(\text{FauciTherm}) + .043(\text{BLMtherm}) + .282(\text{BAplus})\\[.4em]
& = -2.269 + .295(2) - .898(3) + .041(65) + .043(60) + .281(1)\\[.4em]
  & = .733
\end{align*}\]
Finally, evaluate using the cumulative logistic distribution: \(\Lambda(.733) = .68\). Recall that for probit it was .65.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Finding the Effect of \(\Delta x_k\)

Quite similar to probit, the predicted effect of the change in \(x_k\) on \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pr}}(y_i = 1)\) is given by: \[\begin{equation*}
\Lambda(\mathbf{\tilde{x}_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta}) - \Lambda(\mathbf{x_{i}}\boldsymbol{\beta})
\end{equation*}\]
The values of all the variables in the analysis are relevant.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Example
Previously we found that the probability of a Biden vote is .68. What if we change Ideology from 3 to 5? \[\begin{align*}
\mathbf{x_i}\boldsymbol{\beta}& = -2.691 + .295(\text{PoliticalNews}) - .898(\text{Ideology})\\
&  + .041(\text{FauciTherm}) + .043(\text{BLMtherm}) + .282(\text{BAplus})\\[.4em]
& = -2.269 + .295(2) - .898(5) + .041(65) + .043(60) + .281(1)\\[.4em]
  & = -1.063
\end{align*}\] Since \(\Lambda(-1.063)\)= .26, we can calculate the effect of the specified change in Ideology: \[\begin{equation*}
\Lambda(-1.063) - \Lambda(.733)= .26 - .68 \ = \ -.42
\end{equation*}\]
The probability of a Biden vote falls by .42 to .26.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Interpretation with Odds Ratios
Since the model in linear in \(\beta_{k}\): \[\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial \ln \Omega(x)}{\partial x_{k}} = \beta_{k}
\end{equation*}\]

A one-unit change in \(x_{k}\) is associated with a \(\beta_{k}\) change in the log odds ratio.
Thus, a one-unit change in \(x_{k}\) is associated with an \(\exp(\beta_{k})\) change in the odds ratio.
If \(\exp(\beta_{k}) >1\), the odds are \(\exp(\beta_{k})\) times larger. If \(\exp(\beta_{k}) <1\), the odds are \(\exp(\beta_{k})\) times smaller.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Logistic Regression

We can get the coefficients reported as the changes in the odds ratios using the logistic command, rather than logit.
In other words, where logit gives us \(\beta_{k}\), logistic will give us a coefficient that equals \(\exp(\beta_{k})\).
If we use the logistic command but add the option coef, we get the same coefficients as the logit command.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Logistic Regression with Odds Ratios





A one-unit increase in Ideology is associated with decreasing the odds of voting for Biden by a factor of .4073.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Key for Interpretation

Odds ratios can never be negative. Rather than be centered around 0, they are centered around 1.
Why? Because if a ratio is multiplied by 1, it does not change.
Thus, a variable has a negative effect on the odds of the outcome if the change in the ratio is less than 1.
A variable has a positive effect if the odds ratio changes by a factor greater than 1.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Example

Suppose the initial odds of a person voting for Biden are 7 to 3. That is an odds ratio of 2.333 and a probability of \(\frac{7}{7 + 3}\) or .70.
If Ideology increases by 1, the odds ratio would change by a factor of .4073, making it \((2.333)(.4073) = .9052\).
That’s odds of .9052 to 1, which is about .48 in probability terms: \[\begin{equation*}
\frac{.9052}{.9052 + 1} \approx .48
\end{equation*}\]
Predicted probabilities are probably easier to interpret, but some disciplines (e.g. public health) tend to use odds ratios.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Advice

Within the same model, odds ratios do have some value in communicating relative risk for different groups.
Even in fields like health research, however, the use of odds ratios is under question (e.g. article by Norton et al.).
Odds ratios are not comparable across different models or studies.
Predicted probabilities and marginal effects are much more understandable to most audiences.

title: PubPol 779  Dichotomous Dependent Variables
text:
Concluding Points

With dichotomous dependent variables, both the LPM and probit/logit models have virtues.
Probit/logit models are better for unbiased predictions of marginal effects for specific hypothetical cases.
The LPM offers easier interpretation of coefficients.
When RCTs have a dichotomous DV, the LPM is just fine.
